extracted.intended_audience: general literate readers of The Spectator; readers interested in manners, education, marriage, and social conduct
extracted.subtask_description: A set of early-18th-century Spectator essays giving prescriptive guidance on manners, education, public decency, the nature of good‑nature, and how to manage jealousy in marriage. The pieces offer rules, observations, and examples for personal and social conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers: polite behaviour and independence from parental flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper set of instructors should be 'polite in their Behaviour and Method of Teaching' and placed 'into a Condition of being above flattering or fearing the Parents of those they instruct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teachers are above flattery or fear of parents, 'Learning become[s] a Pleasure' and children who have genius for learning will be properly trained; this condition would eliminate pedants and avoid breeding scholars without genius. (Surrounding commentary stresses tenderness, absence of harshness, and that gentle treatment makes children fond of their tutor.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentle, affectionate instruction fosters love of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: A tutor who treats pupils with tenderness, never uses harsh words, and mixes diversion with instruction makes learning pleasurable and creates strong affectionate bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example letter: a fourteen‑year‑old praises a Doctor of Divinity who salutes boys at play, never gives a harsh word, and whose displeasure is considered the greatest punishment. Implicit anti-pattern: harsh, punitive tutors who frighten or flatter parents undermine true learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve decency in public assemblies; sanction sets that disturb
rubrics_metrics.description: Public meetings (opera, play, water-works, etc.) are often disturbed by 'Sets' (groups of whisperers, laughers, footmen) whose business is to draw attention from the entertainment onto themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed measures: those who disturb others should pay at least double for their places; inform women of birth that levity degrades them below their meanest attendants; admonish gentlemen that outward dress ('a fine Coat') is only 'a Livery' if behaviour is low. Examples/anti‑patterns include footmen playing at 'All‑fours' in view of the audience and women forming noisy sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-breeding is imitation of good-nature; real good‑nature preferable
rubrics_metrics.description: Good-breeding is 'nothing else but an Imitation and Mimickry of Good-nature' (affability, complaisance, easiness of temper reduced into an art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exterior shows of humanity are popular when founded on real good‑nature; without real good‑nature they become hypocrisy and, when discovered, make a man more detestable than open impiety. Education may improve good‑nature but cannot produce it where it does not exist naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-nature is more agreeable than wit and essential to social intercourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Good-nature 'is more agreeable in Conversation than Wit' and is necessary to sustain society and conversation; it 'takes off in some measure from the Deformity of Vice' and makes folly and impertinence supportable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that there is no society without good‑nature or some imitation of it; good‑nature gives an amiable air to the countenance and shows virtue in its fairest light. Examples invoked: Xenophon and Salust's portraits of philanthropy and mercy (Cæsar vs Cato).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit pardoning of faults to ordinary commerce, not public justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The pardoning/overlooking of faults (a part of good‑nature) should be 'exercised only in doing our selves Justice, and that too in the ordinary Commerce and Occurrences of Life; for in the publick Administrations of Justice, Mercy to one may be Cruelty to others.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides the boundary between private indulgence and public duty: private clemency is a virtue in daily relations, but officials must not let private mercy undermine public equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware mistaking ill-nature or spite for wit
rubrics_metrics.description: It has become a maxim that 'Good-natured Men are not always Men of the most Wit' because 'Ill-nature among ordinary Observers passes for Wit.' Spiteful sayings gratify petty passions and often receive public laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two causes of the perception: (1) ordinary observers reward ill‑nature because it gratifies; (2) good‑natured people avoid turning misfortunes into ridicule and so forfeit certain easy satirical success. Anti‑pattern: using mockery and exposure of faults to gain a reputation for wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define jealousy and recognise its primary features
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy is 'that Pain which a Man feels from the Apprehension that he is not equally beloved by the Person whom he entirely loves.' It produces doubtfulness, never gives satisfaction, and makes a man's life a pursuit of a secret that destroys happiness if found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jealousy mixes ardent love with suspicion; every gesture is interpreted as evidence; it tends to feed on itself. The essay treats jealousy as a deep, often incurable passion that converts everything it touches into its own nourishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the kinds of men most subject to jealousy
rubrics_metrics.description: Three kinds are especially prone: (1) those conscious of infirmity (weakness, old age, deformity, ignorance), (2) cunning, wary, distrustful men who see plots and designs everywhere, and (3) vicious men whose experience of women's behavior breeds mistrust. Also, jealousy is said to be stronger in warmer climates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains psychological and social roots: low self‑esteem, overrefinement/distrust, or corrupt experience. Geographical observation: jealousy rages most in nations nearer the sun, cooling toward the poles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of jealousy: alienation, provocation of the suspected, and self‑destruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Jealousy 'tends to alienate the Affection which it is so solicitous to engross' by imposing constraints and showing dishonourable opinion; it may also 'draw after it a more fatal Train of Consequences, and makes the Person you suspect guilty of the very Crimes you are so much afraid of.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms: excessive control drives the suspected to find solace in others or contemplate actions they wouldn't otherwise; jealousy can thus create the very infidelity feared. Literary/historical example: Herod and Mariamne story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for wives to ease a jealous husband's mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules: (1) never admire in another what the jealous man does not himself possess; (2) be free and open in conversation—'let in Light upon your Actions'—unravel designs and disclose trifling secrets; (3) show sorrow and affliction at his ill opinion to soften him; (4) as a last resort, a cautious counterfeited jealousy may be used by the very discreet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each rule is illustrated: praising qualities the husband lacks inflames him; secrecy fuels suspicion; a dejected, injured carriage may soften him into pity; counterjealousy is an artifice that 'ought never to be put in Practice' except by those with skill and innocence to cover the deceit. Anti‑pattern: affected coldness and triumphing in a lover's jealousy, which kills affection and invites contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate talents by disposition and application to virtue, not by outward accomplishments alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Good talents and accomplishments 'are valuable, but as they are exerted in the Interest of Virtue, or governed by the Rules of Honour.' One should abstract from natural excellence until one has taken notice of the person's disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: approval based on beauty or wit alone ('meer Beauty, or meer Wit') leads to misplaced admiration; both men and women may misuse natural advantages (men of sense may become coxcombs, beautiful women immodest). The standard is the tendency of a person's gifts to promote what is 'good and honourable.'
